exercises.title: Two drivers is a short
exercises.brief: Build Clash, which outputs 1 when more than one of three enable signals is high. This is a fault detector: its job is to notice the wiring that destroys the parts.
exercises.concept: A bus is a rule rather than a component, and the rule is that exactly one output drives it at a time.
hints: Any pair being high at once is a clash. There are three pairs.

diagnose.prose: Read the row that disagreed. The output is 1 when any two are high together, which includes the row where all three are, so an answer that is only true for exactly two misses that one.

exercises.after: Two enabled outputs on a shared wire is a path from the supply straight to ground through two gates. That is the crowbar current from Part I, and it is why every bus in every machine has a rule about who may drive it.

exercises.title: Exactly one, not at least one
exercises.brief: Build OneHot3, which outputs 1 when exactly one of the three enables is high.
exercises.concept: "At least one" and "exactly one" are different circuits, and a bus needs the second.
hints: At least one, and not more than one.

diagnose.prose: The all-zero row and the all-one row both want 0, for different reasons. An answer that is high on the all-ones row has built "at least one", which is the rule that permits a short.

exercises.after: A real control unit asserts one enable per cycle and this is the assertion that says so. Part III runs checks of exactly this shape during synthesis rather than during simulation.

exercises.title: The bus you can actually build here
exercises.brief: Build Bus3, which puts one of three sources onto a single output, chosen by two select bits. A select of 3 reads the first source again, because three sources do not fill four combinations.
exercises.concept: Inside a chip a shared wire is a multiplexer, because there is nowhere for a second driver to connect and therefore no rule to get wrong.
hints: Two multiplexers on the low bit and one on the high bit, and the spare combination can be anything the specification says.

diagnose.prose: Read which source the failing row wanted. The select is two bits with s1 as the high one, so a select of 2 is s1 high and s0 low, which reads the third source.
Everything you use has to be defined in this file, Mux included.

exercises.after: On a board you would use three drivers and a rule. Inside a chip you use this, because wires are cheap and a short is fatal. Modern chips are almost entirely the second kind.

exercises.title: The capture inside the drive
exercises.brief: Build GatedLoad, a register that captures its input only when both en and cap are high. The output shows what it held coming into the cycle.
exercises.concept: The capture window sits strictly inside the driving window, so the destination has finished before the source lets go.
hints: Both conditions, and then the register you already have.

diagnose.prose: Read the cycle. A design that loads when either signal is high captures while the source may already have stopped driving, which is the bus fault this exercise is about.

exercises.after: Every bus transfer in every machine has this shape: the enable is wide and the capture is narrow, and the narrow one lives inside the wide one.

exercises.title: Moving a value between two registers
exercises.brief: Build Transfer. Register A loads seed when load_a is high. The bus carries A when sel is 0 and seed when sel is 1. Register B loads the bus when load_b is high. Outputs are A, B and the bus, all as of the start of the cycle.
exercises.concept: A transfer is a source enabled onto a wire and a destination capturing from it, and both halves are ordinary parts you have already built.
hints: Two registers and a multiplexer between them. The bus is combinational.

diagnose.prose: Read which of the three outputs disagreed. The bus is not stored, so it changes in the same cycle its inputs do, while the two registers show what they held coming in. Mixing those up makes everything look one cycle out.
The bus feeds B and B does not feed the bus, so the loop you have is not the one the design needs. Check which register the multiplexer is reading.

exercises.after: This is a whole datapath in miniature. Add an address to choose which register, and the next unit has a memory.

exercises.title: An enable that is never two
exercises.brief: Build SafeEnable2, which takes two requests and produces two enables, with the first request winning if both arrive at once.
exercises.concept: Priority is how a design guarantees one driver without needing anyone to promise it.
hints: The second enable is its request, and not the first request.

diagnose.prose: The row where both requests are high is the only interesting one. The first enable is high there and the second is not, which is what makes the pair impossible to get wrong.

exercises.after: Building the guarantee into the circuit beats writing it in a comment. Every interrupt controller and every arbiter is this shape with more inputs.

exercises.title: A clock you can build from nothing stable
exercises.brief: Build Ring3, three inverters in a ring, and observe that it never settles. The specification traces what the simulator computes, which is one flip per cycle because the loop is broken by a flip-flop.
exercises.concept: An oscillator is a circuit with no stable state, and the cheapest one is an odd number of inversions in a loop.
hints: An odd number of inversions round a loop, with the flip-flop making the loop legal here.

diagnose.prose: Three inverters invert an odd number of times, so the value that comes back is the opposite of the one that left. With the flip-flop in the loop that becomes one flip per cycle rather than an oscillation at the speed of the gates.
Without a flip-flop this is a genuine combinational loop, and a real one oscillates rather than settling. That is what makes it useful as a clock and useless as logic.

exercises.after: A ring of inverters on a real chip oscillates at a frequency set by how fast that silicon happens to be, which is why one is often built in on purpose as a way of measuring the process.

exercises.title: What the longest path costs
exercises.brief: Build SlowPath, a chain of four inversions from input to output, and notice that its answer is its input while its depth is four gates.
exercises.concept: The clock period must exceed the longest path between flip-flops, and that path is measured in gates rather than in operations.
hints: Four inversions return the value unchanged. The exercise is about the count, not the function.

diagnose.prose: Correct, and over the budget. The specification wants exactly the four inversions, so a design that folds them away is measuring a different circuit from the one being discussed.
An odd number of inversions gives the opposite of the input. Count them.

exercises.after: Every operation in a machine costs what the slowest one costs, because they all wait for the same edge. Making a machine faster means shortening this path, which is what pipelining does five parts from here by cutting it into pieces with flip-flops between them.
exercises.starter:
chip SlowPath(a) -> out {
  n1 = nand(a, a)
  n2 = nand(n1, n1)
  n3 = nand(n2, n2)
  n4 = nand(n3, n3)
  n5 = nand(n4, n4)
  out = nand(n5, n5)
}
